newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong taking less China gas than expected.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong taking less China gas than expected.

text.p: The China National Offshore Oil Corp (CNOOC) supplied between 1.8 billion and 1.9 billion cubic metres of natural gas to Hong Kong in 1996, a less-than-expected amount, senior company officials said.

Hong Kong electricity generator China Light & Power Co Ltd had contracted to take up to 2.9 billion cubic metres of gas a year from the Yacheng 13-1 field in the South China Sea, CNOOC Vice President Chen Bingqian told Reuters in an interview.
While the Hong Kong generator had not been expected to take the full amount in the first year of supply, demand had still fallen short of expectations, Chen said this week.
"They couldn't take any more... There are various reasons," Chen said. "I'm afraid they can't use as much gas as planned."

Under the take-or-pay terms of the contract to supply gas via a 788 km-long undersea pipeline from Yacheng 13-1, Hong Kong could be liable to pay for gas it did not use, Chen said but added that no such charges had been levied so far.
"The two sides can still discuss the matter," he said.

China began pumping gas to the British colony, which returns to Beijing rule on July 1 this year, in January 1996 under a 20-year guaranteed supply contract intended to give the territory an alternative to coal and nuclear powered plants.
The contract accounts for most of the annual 3.4 billion cubic metres capacity of Yacheng 13-1, developed jointly by CNOOC, Atlantic Richfield Co and Kuwait Foreign Petroleum Exploration Co.

The field's remaining 500 million cubic metres of output capacity is set aside for supply to China's southern island of Hainan, where it is used to produce electricity and to supply a fertiliser factory.
Chen declined to give details of the pricing of the gas piped to Hong Kong, but said sales to the territory earned more than those to Hainan.
"We are supporting Hainan's industry...we sell cheap to Hainan," he said.

Officials in China's southern city of Shenzhen said last September that China Light & Power would take a 35 percent stake in a gas-fired power plant project in the city that would help the Hong Kong company use more of its guaranteed supply from China.
The Shenzhen plant is scheduled to start operation in 1999.
